narrative:
The model estimates a 61% probability that you will fail your final year, meaning that among students with a similar profile, failure is more likely than passing. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it is high enough that remedial courses are being required to give you extra support before the end of the year.

The strongest reason for the prediction is your record of one past class failure, compared with an average of none among students who passed. That single history weighs more heavily than anything else and is the main factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Two other important factors actually work in your favour: your low amount of free time and your intention to pursue higher education both push the prediction toward passing. However, those protective signals are not strong enough to outweigh the past failure signal, so the overall prediction remains on the failing side.

To improve your chances, treat the remedial courses as a chance to close gaps rather than a punishment. Your weekly study time is under two hours, while most passing students study two to five hours, so building a steadier study routine is important. You also report no internet at home and no family educational support, so ask school staff how to access learning resources and structured help. Keep your zero absences, use the remedial support consistently, and discuss with your teachers how to prevent further failures.
